text: Warner Records Inc., formerly known as Warner Bros. Records Inc. until 2019, is an American record label and a subsidiary of Warner Music Group, headquartered in Los Angeles, California. It was founded on March 19, 1958, as the recorded music division of Warner Bros. Pictures. At the end of the silent movie period, Warner Bros. Pictures expanded into publishing and recording to access low-cost music content for its films. In 1928, the studio acquired M. Witmark & Sons, Harms Inc., and a partial interest in New World Music Corp., merging them into the Music Publishers Holding Company (MPHC), which controlled valuable copyrights on works by George and Ira Gershwin and Jerome Kern, earning up to US$2 million annually. In 1930, MPHC paid US$28 million to acquire Brunswick Records (including Vocalion), whose roster included Duke Ellington, Red Nichols, Nick Lucas, Al Jolson, Earl Burtnett, Ethel Waters, Abe Lyman, Leroy Carr, Tampa Red, and Memphis Minnie. After the sale, Warner Bros. signed Bing Crosby, Mills Brothers, and Boswell Sisters. However, the Great Depression and the rise of broadcast radio caused a 90% drop in record sales—from over 100 million in 1927 to fewer than 10 million by 1932—and major companies reduced record prices from 75 to 35 cents. In December 1931, Warner Bros. leased Brunswick to the American Record Corporation (ARC) for a fraction of its value, retaining ownership of the label and its pressing plants; when ARC was sold to CBS in 1939 and Brunswick was discontinued, ownership reverted to Warner Bros. In 1941, Warner Bros. sold Brunswick and its catalog up to 1931, along with its pressing plants, to Decca Records in exchange for a financial interest in Decca, resulting in a significant financial loss that kept the studio out of the record business for nearly 20 years, during which it licensed film music to other companies for soundtrack releases. Warner Bros. returned to the record business on March 19, 1958, establishing Warner Bros. Records. This move followed the decline of the Hollywood studios due to television and legal changes, including anti-trust suits that forced the major studios to divest their cinema chains. In 1956, Harry Warner and Albert Warner sold their interests, and the board included Charles Allen, Serge Semenenko, and David Baird, with Semenenko advocating for an in-house record label. He argued that with record sales exceeding US$500 million by 1958, Warner Bros. could profitably create its own label to exploit its contract actors. The music career of actor Tab Hunter, who achieved success with Dot Records—including the US No. 1 single "Young Love" (1957)—prompted Warner Bros. to sign him as its first artist in 1958, though his later recordings failed to match that success. Warner Bros. had attempted to buy Imperial Records in 1956, a deal that collapsed, but it signaled a shift in mindset: "If the company was willing to buy another label, why not start its own?" The label was established with James B. Conkling as president, and founding A&R directors Harris Ashburn, George Avakian, and Bob Prince. Conkling had experience launching the LP format at Columbia and founding the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, but his middle-of-the-road tastes clashed with the growing rock 'n' roll market. Warner Bros. Records opened on March 19, 1958, with early albums targeting the upscale mainstream and stereo LPs for the "hi-fi" market. Most early releases were commercial failures; the only charting album in the first two years was Warren Barker's soundtrack for 77 Sunset Strip, which reached No. 3 in 1959. Tab Hunter's "Jealous Heart" (WB 5008) reached No. 62, the label's only charting single in its first year. Early singles featured pink labels with the WB logo, "WARNER" in white Hellenic font to the left, "BROS." to the right, and "VITAPHONIC HIGH FIDELITY" in white Rockwell font below. This label was used from 1958 to 1960 and was later replaced by a red label with a WB shield at 9 o'clock and colored arrows. The first hit was "Kookie, Kookie (Lend Me Your Comb)" by Edd Byrnes, with lyrics and music by Irving Taylor, which reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100. Actress and singer Connie Stevens contributed to the chorus, but the label assigned her only a 1% royalty despite her contract granting a 5%, and charged her for recording costs. When Stevens released "Sixteen Reasons" in 1960, Warner Bros. refused to allow her to perform it on Hawaiian Eye or The Ed Sullivan Show, denying her promotion and a $5000 appearance fee. By 1960, the label had lost at least US$3 million and was in serious financial trouble, with music historian Fredric Dannen noting it was saved only because the board refused to write off $2 million in receivables and inventory. After restructuring, Conkling reported to Herman Starr, who rejected a buyout offer and agreed to keep the label running with heavy cost-cutting—staff reduced from 100 to 30 and Conkling cut his salary from $1,000 to $500. Warner Bros. turned to rock 'n' roll, signing Bill Haley, who had passed his prime and failed to hit, but succeeded with the Everly Brothers after their contract with Cadence ended. Herman Starr approved a then-recorded million-dollar contract, guaranteeing the Everly Brothers $525,000 with escalating royalties up to 7%, above industry standards. The duo's first single, "Cathy's Clown," reached No. 1 and sold over eight million copies, and their debut album, It's Everly Time, reached No. 9. In late 1959, Warner Bros. signed Bob Newhart, a Chicago-based comedian unknown outside the region, who had only done local radio and TV work and was still working as an accountant. A friend, DJ Dan Sorkin, connected Newhart to CEO Jim Conkling, who liked his demo. Newhart recorded at The Tidelands in Houston, where he was terrified on his first night but quickly wrote enough material for a full LP. When he asked about the release, he was told the label was rushing copies to Minneapolis after radio DJs broke the album, which became so popular that a local newspaper printed airplay times. The album, The Button-Down Mind of Bob Newhart, reached No. 1 and stayed there for 14 weeks, charting for over two years and selling over 600,000 copies. At the 1961 Grammys, Newhart won Album of the Year, Best Comedy Performance–Spoken Word, and Best New Artist—making it the first comedy album to win Album of the Year and the only time a comedian has won Best New Artist. Newhart recalled that Warner greeted him as "the man who saved Warner Brothers Records" after meeting him. In 1961, Conkling was unexpectedly removed as CEO after it was discovered he had sold his Warner Bros. stock for around $1 million, though biographers Warren Zanes and Stan Cornyn argued this was a pretext, as his successor had been chosen before his termination. Conkling resigned in the fall of 1961 and was replaced by Mike Maitland, a former Capitol Records executive, with Joe Smith appointed head of promotions. Warner Bros. also signed folk group Peter, Paul & Mary, who were about to sign with Atlantic Records but were poached by Warner Bros. through Artie Mogull, who connected their manager Albert Grossman to Herman Starr. The deal included a $30,000 advance and gave the group complete creative control over recordings and packaging—a first for recording artists. Grossman also signed Bob Dylan to Witmark for $5,000, buying out Dylan's previous contract. In 1963, Peter, Paul & Mary scored two consecutive Top 10 hits with Dylan songs, launching Dylan's career and leading to widespread success for artists covering his songs. Grossman earned a 25% commission as Dylan's manager and 50% of Witmark's share of Dylan's publishing income, a model later adopted by others like David Geffen. The label also achieved major success with comedy recordings, including Allan Sherman's debut LP My Son, the Folk Singer (1962), which sold over a million copies and won a Gold Record, cited as the fastest-selling LP in US history, and his single "Hello Muddah, Hello Faddah" (1963), which reached No. 2. Bill Cosby followed with a string of successful comedy albums in the late 1960s. By 1962, the label had turned around commercially and financially, thanks to the Everly Brothers, Newhart, Peter, Paul & Mary, Joanie Sommers, and Sherman, ending the financial year 1961–62 in the black for the first time since its founding. In August 1963, Warner Bros. acquired Frank Sinatra's ailing Reprise Records in a deal valued at around US$10 million, giving Sinatra a one-third share in the combined company and a seat on the board. Mike Maitland became president of the new entity, and Mo Ostin remained as Reprise's manager. Reprise was in debt at the time, and the acquisition pushed the balance sheet into the red, but the deal was non-negotiable due to pressure from Ben Kalmenson, a Warner director and Jack Warner's aide, who told the directors they had to vote in favor. Despite initial concerns, the acquisition proved highly beneficial: Reprise flourished due to Sinatra's comeback and hits by Sinatra and his daughter Nancy, secured US distribution rights to the Kinks and Jimi Hendrix, and most importantly, brought Mo Ostin into the Warner fold, whose value to the company was considered greater than Sinatra's.

Mike Maitland became the president of the new Warner/Reprise combine after the takeover, while Mo Ostin was retained as manager of the Reprise label. Reprise was heavily in debt at the time of the acquisition, and the Warner Records management team was dismayed by the negative impact on their balance sheet, though they had no choice but to support the deal. Ben Kalmenson, a Warner Bros. director and close aide to Jack Warner, summoned the label's directors to a meeting in New York and explicitly told them both he and Warner wanted the deal and expected their approval. Despite initial misgivings, the merger proved highly beneficial, with Reprise flourishing in the late 1960s due to Frank Sinatra's comeback and hits by Sinatra and his daughter Nancy, as well as securing U.S. distribution rights to the Kinks and Jimi Hendrix. Most importantly, the merger brought Mo Ostin into the Warner fold, whose business and musical instincts and rapport with artists proved crucial to the success of the Warner labels over the next two decades. In 1964, Warner Bros. launched Loma Records, run by Bob Krasnow, which released over 100 singles and five albums but saw limited success and was wound down in 1968. Ed Thrasher joined Warner/Reprise in 1964 as head art director, designing covers for the Jimi Hendrix Experience's Are You Experienced, Van Morrison's Astral Weeks, the Grateful Dead's Anthem of the Sun, the Doobie Brothers' Toulouse Street, Tiny Tim's God Bless Tiny Tim, and Joni Mitchell's Clouds, setting a trend of artists creating their own sleeve art. In 1973, Thrasher photographed the cover of Sinatra's comeback album and devised the title Ol' Blue Eyes Is Back, which was widely used in promotion. Thrasher also art-directed many Warner Bros. ads and posters from 1964 to 1979. In 1964, Warner Bros. successfully negotiated with French label Disques Vogue and British distributor Pye Records for the rights to distribute Petula Clark's recordings in the U.S. (previously held by Laurie Records), leading to Clark's No. 1 hit "Downtown," and Warner also released other Pye artists in the U.S., with Pye distributing Warner recordings in the U.K. from 1964 to 1970. In 1966, Mo Ostin hired Lenny Waronker as an A&R manager, beginning a long mentor/protegé relationship. Waronker, son of Liberty Records founder Simon Waronker and former assistant to Snuff Garrett, had worked with Autumn Records, founded by Tom Donahue, Bobby Mitchell, and Sylvester Stewart (later known as Sly Stone). He produced albums for the Tikis (later Harpers Bizarre), the Beau Brummels, and the Mojo Men, bringing in musician friends like Randy Newman, Leon Russell, and Van Dyke Parks, who became the foundation of a creative salon at Warner Bros. that contributed to the label's rock success. Initially, Waronker managed acts acquired when Warner bought Autumn Records for $10,000, and he actively pursued Buffalo Springfield, though the band was signed by Atlantic and later joined the Warner catalog after Atlantic was acquired. In 1967, Warner Bros. acquired Valiant Records, adding the hit-making harmony pop group the Association to its roster. The Association scored major hits in the late 1960s, with "Never My Love" becoming the second-most-played song on American radio and TV in the 20th century. Warner also signed the Grateful Dead in 1967, hosting a release party at Fugazi Hall in San Francisco's North Beach, where A&R manager Joe Smith announced the signing, prompting Jerry Garcia to quip that it was an honor for the Grateful Dead to introduce Warner Bros. to the world. In the same year, Warner/Reprise established Warner Reprise Canada Ltd., replacing its distribution deal with Compo Company, marking the origin of Warner Music Canada. In November 1966, the entire Warner group was acquired by Seven Arts Productions, owned by Eliot Hyman, for US$32 million, a move that stunned the film world and was described by Warner executive Joe Smith as "as if the Pasadena Star-News bought The New York Times." The merged company was renamed Warner Bros.-Seven Arts, or "W7," and despite Warner Bros. Pictures' struggles, the music division experienced tremendous growth. Hyman's investment banker Alan Hirshfeld urged expansion and arranged a meeting with Jerry Wexler and the Ertegun brothers of Atlantic Records, leading to the purchase of Atlantic in 1968. In June 1967, Mo Ostin attended the Monterey International Pop Festival, where the Association performed. Ostin had already acquired the U.S. rights to the Jimi Hendrix Experience's recordings, but was unimpressed by Hendrix's performance. He met Andy Wickham, who worked with Lou Adler and Dunhill Records, and hired him as Warner's "house hippie" for $200 per week. Wickham scouted talent and established rapport with young musicians, helping to sign Eric Andersen, Jethro Tull, Van Morrison, and Joni Mitchell (who signed to Reprise). Over the next thirty years, Wickham became a key A&R manager, signing Emmylou Harris, Buck Owens, and a-ha. Warner Bros. also signed Randy Newman and Van Dyke Parks. Newman achieved industry recognition through songs covered by other acts like Three Dog Night and Alan Price, while Parks, a respected session musician and collaborator with Brian Wilson on the unreleased Beach Boys album Smile, released his Warner debut album Song Cycle in 1967, which cost over $35,000 to produce and sold poorly despite critical acclaim. Publicist Stan Cornyn ran a tongue-in-cheek ad claiming the label had "lost $35,509 on 'the album of the year'" and offered to exchange worn copies for two new ones, incensing Parks, who accused Cornyn of trying to kill his career. Cornyn also faced backlash with Joni Mitchell when a tagline "Joni Mitchell is 90% Virgin" reportedly reduced her to tears and was withdrawn. The Grateful Dead, like Peter, Paul and Mary, negotiated complete artistic control over their recordings and packaging. Their debut album, recorded in four days, cracked the U.S. Top 50 and went gold in 1971. For their second album, they undertook a seven-month recording process from September 1967 to March 1968, starting with David Hassinger, who quit in December 1967, and later took over production with the band and sound engineer Dan Healy, intermixing studio and concert recordings. Anthem of the Sun was the least successful of their 1960s albums, sold poorly, and cost the label over $100,000, with Joe Smith calling it "the most unreasonable project with which we have ever involved ourselves." For Aoxomoxoa (1969), the band took another seven months and spent $180,000, which sold poorly and took nearly thirty years to achieve gold status. In 1971, the band proposed a live double album titled Skull Fuck, which Ostin diplomatically handled by reminding them of their debt and that the provocative title would hurt sales due to retailers like Sears refusing to stock it. The band changed the title to Grateful Dead, known as Skull and Roses. Warner Bros.' biggest commercial successes included Harpers Bizarre's No. 13 hit in April 1967 with "The 59th Street Bridge Song (Feelin' Groovy)" and the Association's No. 1 hit "Windy" and No. 8 album chart entry with Insight Out, followed by "Never My Love" topping the charts in autumn 1967 (No. 2 Billboard, No. 1 Cashbox), now recognized as one of the most successful Warner recordings and the second most-played song on U.S. radio in the 20th century. The Association's 1968 Greatest Hits album reached No. 4 on the U.S. album chart. In 1968, Mason Williams' "Classical Gas" reached No. 2 on the Billboard chart, selling over a million copies, and Williams won three Grammys. Van Morrison's Astral Weeks, released in 1968, sold poorly initially and did not reach gold status until 2001, but has been widely acclaimed and remains in continuous release. In 1968, using profits from Warner/Reprise, W7 purchased Atlantic Records for $17.5 million, including its archive, artist roster, and executives Jerry Wexler, Ahmet Ertegun, and Nesuhi Ertegun. The deal caused rancor among Warner/Reprise management, who were upset that their profits were used to buy Atlantic and that the Ertegun brothers and Wexler received 66,000 shares of Warner Bros. common stock. On June 1, 1968, Billboard reported that Bill Cosby declined a five-year, US$3.5 million contract renewal and would leave Warner Bros. to record for his own Tetragrammaton Records. Just over a month later, on July 13, a major reorganization of the Warner-Seven Arts music division was announced: Mike Maitland was promoted to Executive Vice-President of both recorded music and publishing, and George Lee replaced Victor Blau as operational head of the recording division. The restructure reversed the 1960 reporting arrangement, with the publishing arm now reporting to the record division under Maitland. The article noted that W7's music operations had grown significantly, generating 74% of the corporation's total profit in the first nine months of the fiscal year, with the publishing division alone accounting for over US$2 million in ASCAP collections. In 1969, Warner Bros.-Seven Arts was taken over by Kinney National Company, led by Steve J. Ross, who would lead the Warner group until his death in 1992. The US$400 million deal created a new conglomerate combining Warner's film, television, recording, and music publishing divisions with Kinney's holdings. Ross founded Kinney in the late 1950s through a car hire operation and later merged it with the Kinney parking garage company, going public in 1962. Between 1966 and 1968, Kinney expanded rapidly by merging with National Cleaning Services in 1966 to form Kinney National Company and acquiring National Periodical Publications (including DC Comics and All American Comics), the Ashley-Famous talent agency, and Panavision. In the summer of 1969, Atlantic agreed to assist Warner in establishing overseas divisions, but when Warner executive Phil Rose arrived in Australia to set up a subsidiary, he discovered that Atlantic had signed a four-year production and distribution deal with local label Festival Records without informing Warner Bros. During 1969, a rivalry between Mike Maitland and Ahmet Ertegun escalated into an executive battle, though Steve Ross favored Ertegun.

Steve Ross founded a successful car hire operation using his family's idle funeral business cars, later merging it with the Kinney parking garage company. He took the company public in 1962, and from this base it expanded rapidly between 1966 and 1968, merging with National Cleaning Services in 1966 to form the Kinney National Company, and then acquiring National Periodical Publications (which included DC Comics and All American Comics), the Ashley-Famous talent agency, and Panavision. In the summer of 1969, Atlantic Records agreed to assist Warner Bros. Records in establishing overseas divisions, but when Warner executive Phil Rose arrived in Australia to begin setting up a subsidiary, he discovered that just one week earlier Atlantic had signed a new four-year production and distribution deal with local label Festival Records without informing Warner Bros. During 1969, the rivalry between Mike Maitland and Ahmet Ertegun escalated into an all-out executive battle, but Steve Ross favored Ertegun, and the conflict culminated in Maitland being dismissed from his position on January 25, 1970. He declined an offer of a job with Warner Bros. Pictures and left the company, subsequently becoming president of MCA Records. Mo Ostin was appointed president of Warner Bros. Records with Joe Smith as executive vice-president. In 1970, the 'Seven Arts' name was dropped and the WB shield became the Warner Bros. Records logo again. During 1972, a financial scandal in its parking operations forced Kinney National to spin off its non-entertainment assets, and the Warner recording, publishing and film divisions then became part of a new umbrella company, Warner Communications. In July 1970, the Warner recording group acquired another prestige asset with the purchase of Jac Holzman's Elektra Records for US$10 million. Like Atlantic, the new acquisition came with a very valuable back-catalogue, which included the Doors, Love, Paul Butterfield Blues Band, Tim Buckley, the Stooges, MC5 and Bread, but Elektra soon began producing more major hits under the Warner umbrella. Recent signing Carly Simon scored two successive Top 20 singles in 1971 with "That's the Way I've Always Heard It Should Be" and "Anticipation", and her first two albums both made the Billboard Top 50, but the following year she topped the single and album charts with her international smash hit "You're So Vain" and the album No Secrets, which both went to No. 1 in the US. Jac Holzman ran the label until 1972, when he was succeeded by David Geffen and Elektra was merged with Geffen's label Asylum Records. Geffen was forced to step down in 1975 for health reasons and Joe Smith was appointed president in his place, although the label's fortunes subsequently waned considerably, with Elektra-Asylum reportedly losing some $27 million during the last two years of Smith's tenure. With three co-owned record companies, the next step was the formation of the group's in-house distribution arm, initially called Kinney Records Distributing Corporation, to better control distribution of product and make sure records by breaking new acts were available. In 1971, UK-based pop rock trio America were signed to the recently established British division of Warner Bros. Their debut album, released late in the year, at first enjoyed only moderate success, but in early 1972 their single "A Horse with No Name" became a major international hit, reaching No. 1 in the US. Warner hastily reissued the album with the song included and it too became a huge hit, reaching No. 1 on the US album chart and eventually earning a platinum record award. Although criticized for their similarity to Neil Young (indeed, rumors circulated around Hollywood that Young had cut the track anonymously), America scored five more US Top 10 singles over the next three years, including a second US No. 1 with "Sister Golden Hair" in 1975. Their albums performed very strongly in the charts—each of their first seven albums were US Top 40 albums, five of these made the Top 10 and all but one (Hat Trick, 1973) achieved either gold or platinum status. Their 1975 Greatest Hits album became a perennial seller and is now accredited at 4× platinum. In 1972, Dionne Warwick was signed to Warner Bros. Records after leaving Scepter Records in what was the biggest contract at the time for a female recording artist, although her five years at Warner Bros. were relatively unsuccessful in comparison to her spectacular hit-making tenure at Scepter. After a slow start, the Doobie Brothers proved to be one of Warner Bros.' most successful signings. Their debut album made little impact but their second album Toulouse Street (1972) reached No. 21 and spawned two US Top 40 singles, "Listen to the Music" and "Jesus is Just Alright", inaugurating a string of hit albums and singles over the next five years. Their third album The Captain and Me was even more successful, reaching No. 7 in the US and producing two more hit singles, "China Grove" (#15) and "Long Train Runnin'" (#8); it became a consistent seller and is now accredited 2× Platinum by the RIAA. What Were Once Vices Are Now Habits (1974) reached No. 4 and produced two more hits including their first US No. 1 single "Black Water" (1975). Stampede also reached No. 4, and produced another hit single with the Motown cover "Take Me in Your Arms (Rock Me a Little While)" (US #11). Warner Bros. Records' reputation for nurturing new artists was demonstrated by the career of Alice Cooper (originally the name of the band, but later taken over as the stage name / persona of singer and main songwriter Vince Furnier). The Alice Cooper band recorded two unsuccessful albums for Frank Zappa's Warner-distributed label Straight Records before teaming with producer Bob Ezrin, who became a longtime collaborator. Their third LP Love it to Death (originally released on Straight and later reissued on Warner Bros.) reached No. 35 on the Billboard album chart and produced the hit single "I'm Eighteen", which reached No. 21. Following the runaway success of their 1971 European tour Warner Bros. Records offered the band a multi-album contract; their first Warner Bros. album Killer sold well, with the single "Halo of Flies" making the Top 10 in the Netherlands, but it was their next album School's Out (1972) that really put them on the map. The title song was a Top 10 hit in the US, reached No. 1 in the UK and became a radio staple, and the album went to No. 2 in the US and sold more than a million copies. Billion Dollar Babies (1973) became their biggest success, going to No. 1 in both the US and the UK. The follow-up Muscle of Love (1973) was less successful, although the single "Teenage Lament '74" was a Top 20 hit in the UK. Furnier split from the band in 1974 and signed to Warner Bros.' sister label, Atlantic as a solo artist, scoring further success with his solo albums and singles. In 1973, Frank Zappa and manager Herb Cohen closed the Straight and Bizarre labels and established a new imprint, DiscReet Records, retaining their distribution deal with Warner Bros. Zappa's next album Apostrophe (') (1973) became the biggest commercial success of his career, reaching No. 10 on the Billboard album chart, and the single "Don't Eat the Yellow Snow" was a minor hit and (at the time) his only single to make the Hot 100 chart. Zappa also enjoyed moderate commercial success with the live double album Roxy and Elsewhere (1974) and his next studio album One Size Fits All (1975), both of which reached the Top 30 on the Billboard album chart. WBR introduced a new label design for its LPs and singles in mid-1973. This design, which WBR would use until mid-1978, featured a multi-colored, idealized watercolor painting of a Burbank street lined by palms and eucalypts, and titled with the slogan "Burbank, Home of Warner Bros. Records". According to the label's official history, the design was copied from a similarly styled "orange crate art" fruit company label illustration created by an unknown commercial artist in the 1920s. After several years as a 'cult' artist, Randy Newman achieved his first significant commercial success as a solo artist with his 1974 album Good Old Boys which made the Top 40. His controversial 1977 single "Short People" was one of the surprise hits of the year, reaching No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100. On October 12, 1974, WBR and Phil Spector established Warner-Spector Records, but the label was short-lived and folded in 1977; most of its releases were reissues Philles Records recordings from the 1960s and the only new material released was two singles by the disco group Calhoon and a single by Cher. In 1975 David Geffen was obliged to leave the company for health reasons, after being told that he had a terminal illness (although this later proved to be a false diagnosis). In his place, Joe Smith was promoted to become President of the combined Elektra/Asylum label. At this time Warner Bros. began to wind down the Reprise label. In 1976–77 almost all Reprise acts, including Fleetwood Mac, Gordon Lightfoot, Ry Cooder and Michael Franks were transferred to Warner Bros., leaving only Neil Young (who refused to move) and founder Frank Sinatra. Apart from these artists and some reissues, the Reprise label was dormant until it was reactivated in 1986 with the issue of the Dream Academy's single "The Love Parade" on Reprise 28750. By far the most successful of the Reprise acts who moved to Warner Bros. was Fleetwood Mac, whose massive success firmly established Warner Bros. in the front rank of major labels—although few would have predicted it from the band's tumultuous history. Between 1970 and 1975 there were multiple lineup changes (with only two original members remaining by 1974), their album sales declined drastically, and a legal battle over the group's name kept them off the road for over a year. However, just as Fleetwood Mac was switching labels in 1975, the group re-invigorated by the recruitment of new members Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks. The 'new' Fleetwood Mac scored a string of US and international hits and their self-titled Reprise debut album was a huge success, reaching No. 1 in the US, charting for more than 30 weeks and selling more than 5 million copies. In 1977, their now-legendary Rumours took both group and Warner Bros. label to even greater heights—it generated a string of international hit singles and became the most successful album in the label's history; it is currently ranked the 11th biggest selling album of all time and as of 2009 was estimated to have sold more than 40 million copies. After a string of albums with the Faces and as a solo artist for Mercury Records in the early 1970s, British singer Rod Stewart signed with Warner Bros. in 1974, applied for American citizenship and moved to the US. Launching a sustained run of success, his Warner debut album Atlantic Crossing (1975) was a major international hit, reaching No. 9 on the Billboard album chart and No. 1 in Australia, with the single "I Don't Want to Talk About It" going to No. 1 in the UK. His second WBR album A Night on the Town (1976) went to No. 2 in the US and No. 1 in Australia and produced three US Top 40 singles, including his first US No. 1 "Tonight's the Night". Foot Loose & Fancy Free (1977) reached No. 2 on the Billboard Pop Albums chart and No. 1 in Australia and again produced three US Top 40 singles, including "You're in My Heart (The Final Acclaim)", which reached No. 4. Blondes Have More Fun (1978) went to No. 1 in the US and Australia, and produced two more Top 40 singles including his second US No. 1, "Da Ya Think I'm Sexy?" (although Stewart and co-writer Carmine Appice were later successfully sued for plagiarizing the song's catchy melody hook from "Taj Mahal" by Brazilian songwriter Jorge Ben). Stewart's Greatest Hits collection (1979) went to No. 1 in the UK and Australia, giving the singer a record-breaking five consecutive No. 1 albums in the latter country. Warner Bros. Records also had unexpected success in the mid-1970s with another 'heritage' act, veteran vocal group the Four Seasons. In early 1975, they signed with Curb Records (which was distributed by WBR) just as lead singer Frankie Valli scored a surprise hit with his independently released solo single "My Eyes Adored You". Soon after, Valli and The Four Seasons burst back onto the charts with the disco-styled "Who Loves You", which reached No. 3 in the US and sold more than a million copies, and the album Who Loves You sold more than 1 million copies. Their next single "December 1963 (Oh, What a Night)" topped the charts in both Britain and the US in early 1976, becoming the group's first US No. 1 since 1967. A remixed version was a hit again in 1994 and its total of 54 weeks in charts gives it the longest tenure of any song on the Billboard Hot 100. By the time of the Doobie Brothers 1976 album Takin' It to the Streets, founding member Tom Johnston had effectively left the band and he was replaced by former Steely Dan session man Michael McDonald, whose distinctive voice helped to propel the group to even greater success. The new album sold strongly, reaching No. 8 in the US, and the title track reached No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100, becoming a perennial on radio playlists. Warner Bros. also released the massively successful Best of the Doobies (1976), which has become one of the biggest-selling albums of all time and is currently accredited at 10× Platinum status. 1978's Minute by Minute marked the peak of their career—both the album and its lead single "What A Fool Believes" were major successes.

"3 (Oh, What a Night)" reached the top of the charts in both Britain and the US in early 1976, marking the Doobie Brothers' first US No. 1 since 1967. A remixed version of the song became a hit again in 1994, and its total of 54 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100 gives it the longest chart tenure of any song on the list. By the time of the 1976 album *Takin' It to the Streets*, founding member Tom Johnston had effectively left the band and was replaced by former Steely Dan session man Michael McDonald, whose distinctive voice contributed to the group's increased success. The album sold well, reaching No. 8 in the US, and its title track reached No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100, becoming a perennial on radio playlists. Warner Bros. also released *Best of the Doobies* (1976), which became one of the biggest-selling albums of all time and is currently accredited at 10× Platinum. In 1978, *Minute by Minute* reached the peak of the band's career, with both the album and its lead single "What A Fool Believes" going to No. 1 in the US, and the album's title track entering the US Top 20; it was also their last album featuring founding drummer John Hartman and long-serving guitarist Jeff "Skunk" Baxter. During the late 1970s, Warner Bros.' reputation as an "artists first" label was challenged by a prolonged dispute with Frank Zappa. In 1976, Zappa's relationship with manager Herb Cohen ended in litigation. For *Zoot Allures*, Zappa took his master copy directly to Warner Bros. Records, who agreed to release it, bypassing Cohen and DiscReet. However, after legal action from Cohen, Warner Bros. changed its position and required Zappa to deliver four more albums for release on DiscReet. Zappa produced a double live album and three studio albums, but Warner Bros. objected to some or all of the recordings and refused to reimburse Zappa for production costs as required by the DiscReet contract. Zappa then re-edited the material into a 4-LP set called *Läther* (pronounced 'leather'), made a deal with Phonogram, and scheduled its release for Halloween 1977. Warner Bros. threatened legal action, forcing Zappa to shelve the release. Infuriated, Zappa hosted a broadcast on KROQ-FM in Pasadena, California, where he played the entire *Läther* album in sequence, repeatedly criticizing Warner Bros. and openly encouraging listeners to record it. Warner Bros. took further legal action, preventing Zappa from issuing any material for over a year. Between 1978 and 1979, Warner Bros. released the disputed material across four albums: *Zappa in New York* (an edited and censored version of the original 1977 live double album), *Studio Tan*, *Sleep Dirt*, and *Orchestral Favorites*. Zappa eventually won the rights to his Straight, Bizarre, DiscReet, and Warner Bros. material, but remained critically opposed to his treatment by the label for the rest of his life. Zappa's recordings were later reissued on CD by Rykodisc (ironically, the label was later acquired by Warner Music), including *Läther*, which appeared posthumously in 1996. Ry Cooder, another Reprise act, was transferred to Warner Bros. in 1977. His first Warner release was the 1977 live album *Showtime*, and he remained with the label until his contract expired in the late 1980s. His 1979 album *Bop 'Til You Drop* is notable as the first major-label rock album to be digitally recorded and became the best-selling album of his career. Thanks to its distribution deal with Curb Records, Warner Bros. Records achieved its biggest hit single in the company's history in 1977: "You Light Up My Life" (written and produced by Joe Brooks), originally recorded by Kasey Cisyk for the film of the same name, with Didi Conn lip-synching to Cisyk's version. Teenager Debby Boone (daughter of actor-singer Pat Boone) was recruited to record a new version, which became a massive success, topping the Billboard Hot 100 for a record-setting 10 consecutive weeks and earning platinum certification from the RIAA. It became the most successful single of the 1970s in the United States, setting a new record for the longest run at No. 1 in the US and surpassing Elvis Presley's "Hound Dog." Boone's success earned her Grammy nominations for "Best Female Pop Vocal Performance" and "Record of the Year," and she won the 1977 Grammy for "Best New Artist" and the 1977 American Music Award for "Favorite Pop Single." The song also earned Joe Brooks the 1977 "Song of the Year" Grammy (tied with "Evergreen (Love Theme from A Star Is Born)") and "Best Original Song" at both the 1977 Golden Globe and Academy Awards. Throughout the 1970s, Warner Bros. benefited from its US/Canada distribution deals with independent labels such as Straight Records, DiscReet Records, UK labels Chrysalis (1972–1976) and Island (1974–1982), Bizarre Records, Bearsville Records (1970–1984), and Geffen Records (sold to MCA in 1990). Although primarily associated with mainstream white acts in the 1970s, Warner Bros.' distribution deals with smaller labels also brought success in the disco, soul, and funk genres in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Notable imprints included Seymour Stein's Sire Records (which Warner Bros. soon purchased), Curtis Mayfield's Curtom, Norman Whitfield's Whitfield Records, Quincy Jones' Qwest, Prince's Paisley Park, RFC Records (formed in December 1978 when Ray Caviano became executive director of Warner's disco division), and Tom Silverman's Tommy Boy Records (another label Warner Bros. eventually took over). Until the late 1970s, Warner Bros. had very few Black artists on its roster, but this began to change with the signing of George Benson and Prince. Benson had risen to prominence in jazz in the 1960s but was relatively unknown to the general public. His move to Warner Bros. in 1976 and collaboration with producer Tommy LiPuma enabled him to cross genres and become a popular and highly successful mainstream R&B and pop artist. His first Warner Bros. album, *Breezin'* (1976), became one of the most successful jazz albums of the decade and a major crossover hit—topping the American Pop, R&B, and Jazz album charts and producing two hit singles: the title track (which became a Jazz standard and a radio favorite) and "This Masquerade," a Top 10 pop and R&B hit. All of Benson's Warner albums made the Top 20 on the US jazz album chart, and beginning with *Breezin'*, he scored seven consecutive US No. 1 jazz albums; the first five of these were also Top 20 hits on both the Pop and R&B charts. His live version of Leiber & Stoller's "On Broadway" (from his 1978 live album *Weekend in L.A.*) outcharted the original by the Drifters, reaching No. 7 on the Billboard Hot 100, and gained further exposure through its use in the famous audition sequence in Bob Fosse's 1979 film *All That Jazz*. Benson's most successful single, "Give Me the Night" (1980), became his first US No. 1 R&B hit, reached No. 4 on the Pop chart, and also reached No. 2 on the Hot Disco Singles chart. Prince signed with Warner Bros. in 1977. His first album, *For You*, had little impact, though the single "Soft and Wet" reached No. 12 on the Billboard R&B chart. His second self-titled album (1979) reached No. 3 on the R&B album chart and earned a gold record award; the first single, "I Wanna Be Your Lover," became Prince's first crossover hit, reaching No. 1 on the R&B chart and No. 11 on the main pop chart, while the follow-up single "Why You Wanna Treat Me So Bad?" reached No. 13 on the R&B chart. Although little known outside the US at the time, this early success laid the foundation for his major commercial breakthrough in the 1980s. Another valuable late 1970s discovery was the metal-pop band Van Halen, spotted at a Hollywood club by Mo Ostin and Ted Templeman in 1977. Their self-titled debut album reached No. 19 on the Billboard album chart, and their second album *Van Halen II* (1979) reached No. 6 and produced their first hit single, "Dance the Night Away" (#19). Warner Bros. also began to embrace the emerging new wave movement in the late 1970s, signing cult bands Devo and the B-52s. A crucial acquisition in this field was the New York-based Sire Records, founded in 1966 by Seymour Stein and Richard Gottehrer. Warner Bros. took over Sire's distribution from ABC Records in 1977 and purchased the label in 1978, retaining Stein as president. The addition of the Sire roster gave Warner Bros. a strong foothold in the new wave scene; Stein is often credited with naming the genre to replace the term "punk," which he disliked. Sire's American signings included the Ramones, the Dead Boys, Talking Heads, and most importantly, Madonna, who soon became the most successful female artist in music history, earning billions for Warner. Sire's distribution deals with British independent labels including Mute, Rough Trade, Korova, and Fiction gave WEA the American rights to important UK-based New Wave bands such as Depeche Mode, the Smiths, the Beat, Madness, Echo & the Bunnymen, and the Cure. Into the 1990s, the label continued to succeed with artists such as Seal, k.d. lang, Tommy Page, Ice-T, and Ministry. In the late 1970s, Warner Bros. also achieved mainstream pop hits with singer/actor Shaun Cassidy—his version of "Da Doo Ron Ron" reached No. 1 in the US in 1977, and his next two singles (both penned by Eric Carmen) were US Top 10 hits, earning him a Grammy nomination. As the decade ended, new acts brought further breakthroughs. Rickie Lee Jones' self-titled debut album reached No. 3 in the US, No. 1 in Australia, and No. 18 in the UK, producing two hit singles: "Chuck E.'s In Love" (US #4) and "Young Blood" (US #40). Thanks to its American distribution deal with Vertigo, British group Dire Straits provided another sustained run of hit albums and singles in the late 1970s and 1980s. Their eponymous debut album (1978) was a surprise international hit, reaching No. 2 in the US and earning a gold record award from the RIAA, while the single "Sultans of Swing" reached No. 4 in the US. Their second album *Communiqué* (1979) made the Top 20 in many countries and earned another gold record award in the US. Warner Bros. also enjoyed renewed success with comedy recordings during this period, transferring Richard Pryor from Reprise and signing rising star Steve Martin, whose second Warner album *A Wild and Crazy Guy* (1978) became one of the label's biggest comedy hits—it reached No. 2 on the pop album chart, won the 1979 Grammy for 'Best Comedy Album,' and Martin's novelty single "King Tut" was a US Top 20 hit. In the 1970s, there were different systems for four-channel stereo. Warner Records and the entire WEA group chose JVC's and RCA's discrete system called CD-4 or Quadradisc, which had the highest separation between the four channels but required a special stylus capable of reading frequencies up to 48,000 Hz. The 1980s marked a period of unprecedented success for Warner Bros. Records. The golden decade began with singer-songwriter Christopher Cross, whose self-titled debut album reached No. 6 in the US and produced four charting singles, including the No. 1 hit "Sailing." He won five major categories at the 1981 Grammy Awards, becoming the only solo artist to win the "Big Four" awards in one year (Record, Song, and Album of the Year, and Best New Artist), while his performance of "Arthur's Theme" from the Dudley Moore film *Arthur*, which also reached No. 1, won both the Oscar and the Golden Globe for Best Original Song. Warner Bros. scored an apparent coup in 1980 by luring Paul Simon away from Columbia Records. His first Warner album, *One Trick Pony* (1980), accompanied the film of the same name, which Simon wrote and starred in. The single "Late in the Evening" was a major hit (#6), but the album was not a big seller. His next album, *Hearts and Bones* (1983), was well received by critics but neither it nor the lead single "Allergies" made the chart, and Simon's career took a nosedive, with the label's patience eventually paying off years later. After two moderate-selling albums that established them as one of the most original American new wave bands of the period, DEVO broke through to mainstream success in 1980 with their third album *Freedom of Choice*, which reached No. 22 in the US. Thanks to its quirky music video, which was heavily promoted on MTV, the single "Whip It" reached No. 14 on the Billboard pop chart, becoming the group's biggest American hit. Their follow-up EP *DEV-O Live* (1981) was a surprise hit in Australia, topping the singles chart for three weeks, but their subsequent albums and singles saw declining sales, and the group was eventually dropped by the label after their 1984 album *Shout*. Prince's 1980 album *Dirty Mind* was widely praised by critics and earned a gold record award, but his 1982 double-LP *1999* became his first major hit album, selling over six million copies and spawning three hit singles. The title track reached No. 12 in the US and provided his first international hit (#25 UK), while his next two singles, "Little Red Corvette" and "Delirious," were both US Top 10 hits. Chicago was picked up by Warner Bros. in 1981 after being dropped by Columbia, which believed the band was no longer commercially viable. After teaming with producer David Foster, the band returned to the charts in 1982 with *Chicago 16*, which reached No. 9 and produced two hit singles, including the US No. 1 hit "Hard To Say I'm Sorry." The group's second Warner album, *Chicago 17*, became the biggest seller of its career—reaching No. 4 in the US and producing four US Top-20 singles, including the Top-5 hits "Hard Habit to Break" (#3) and "You're the Inspiration" (#3), and is currently accredited at 6× Platinum. Lead singer Peter Cetera left the group after this album but continued to have success as a solo artist for Warner, scoring a No. 1 hit in 1986 with "Glory of Love" (from the movie *The Karate Kid Part II*), which was also nominated for a Grammy, Golden Globe, and Academy Award. His second solo album sold over a million copies and produced another No. 1 hit, "The Next Time I Fall." His third solo album produced the Top 5 hit "One Good Woman" (1988) and "After All" reached No. 6. Lenny Waronker took over as President of WBR in 1982, and his first act was to sign Elvis Costello. Costello's first Warner album, *Spike*, featured his biggest American single, the Paul McCartney collaboration "Veronica," which was a US Top 20 hit. He recorded three more critically praised albums for Warner Bros.—*Mighty Like A Rose*, *Brutal Youth*, and *All This Useless Beauty*—but was dropped from the label after the major corporate shakeup in the mid-1990s. After ending his contracts with RSO Records and Polydor, Eric Clapton signed with Warner Bros. in 1982. His first WBR album, *Money and Cigarettes* (1983), reached No. 16 on the Billboard album chart, and the single "I've Got a Rock 'n' Roll Heart" reached No. 18 on the Billboard Hot 100. His next album, *Behind the Sun*, reached No. 34, and the hit single "Forever Man" went to No. 26, though he transferred to Reprise for his next release. Another resurgent 1970s act who achieved major success with Warner Bros. in this period was ZZ Top, which had previously been signed to London Records. During an extended break in the late 1970s, the group gained ownership of its London recordings and signed with Warner Bros., which also re-issued the band's back-catalogue. The group's first two Warner albums, *Deguello* (1979) and *El Loco* (1981), were moderately successful, but *Eliminator* (1983) became a major hit due to strong support from music videos on MTV. The band scored three.

Eric Clapton signed with Warner Bros. in 1982; his first WBR album, Money and Cigarettes (1983), reached No. 16 on the Billboard album chart, and the single "I've Got a Rock 'n' Roll Heart" reached No. 18 on the Billboard Hot 100. His next album, Behind the Sun, reached No. 34 and the single "Forever Man" went to No. 26, after which he transferred to Reprise. ZZ Top, previously signed to London Records, signed with Warner Bros. during an extended break in the late 1970s after gaining ownership of its London recordings, and the label re-issued the band's back-catalogue. Their first two Warner albums, Deguello (1979) and El Loco (1981), were moderately successful, but Eliminator (1983) became a major hit due to strong MTV support, reaching No. 9 on the Billboard 200 and selling in huge numbers, earning a Diamond record award in 1996; the album produced three US hit singles, including "Legs" (US #8). Afterburner (1985) reached No. 4 and produced five hit singles, including "Sleeping Bag" (#8). Madonna's 1983 self-titled debut album and her first mainstream hit single "Holiday" reached No. 16 in the US and became a hit in many other countries, including Australia and the UK (Top 5), with the album making the Top 20 in more than a dozen countries and being certified 5× Platinum. Her follow-up, Like a Virgin, became her first US No. 1 album and has sold over 21 million copies worldwide; the title track reached No. 1 in Australia, Canada, Japan, and the US. "Crazy For You" (1985) became her second US No. 1 hit, and "Material Girl" reached No. 2 in the US and was Top 5 in many other countries. Prince's 1984 film and album Purple Rain sold more than thirteen million copies in the US (25 million worldwide), spent twenty-four consecutive weeks at number one on the Billboard 200, won the Academy Award for "Best Original Song Score," and grossed over $80 million in the US; singles "When Doves Cry" and "Let's Go Crazy" both reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, and the title track reached No. 2. The sexually explicit track "Darling Nikki" caused controversy when politician Tipper Gore, concerned about her daughter listening to it, led to the formation of the Parents Music Resource Center (PMRC), which opposed the practice of explicit lyrics and eventually prompted the US recording industry to adopt the "Parental Advisory: Explicit Lyrics" sticker. In 1984, Van Halen broke into the mainstream with the single "Jump" (their only US No. 1 hit) and the album 1984, which reached No. 2 in the US and earned Diamond status in 1999, producing two more Top 20 hits; however, escalating friction between Eddie Van Halen and David Lee Roth led to Roth's departure and his replacement by Sammy Hagar, who recorded for WB as part of Montrose; 1984 was also the last time they worked with Ted Templeman, who had produced all their albums up to that point. In 1985, Dire Straits' single "Money for Nothing" gained massive exposure on MTV, reaching No. 1 in the US; they scored two more US Top 20 hits with "Walk of Life" and "So Far Away," and the album Brothers in Arms went to No. 1 in the US, Australia, and most European countries, selling over 30 million copies worldwide and being certified 9× platinum in the US by 1996, currently ranked at No. 25 in the list of best-selling albums of all time. The new Van Halen released the successful 5150 album in 1986, which reached No. 1 and produced two hit singles, "Why Can't This Be Love" (US #3) and "Dreams" (#22); their three subsequent studio albums (OU812, For Unlawful Carnal Knowledge, and Balance) all reached No. 1 and the band scored 17 US Top 20 singles, including "When It's Love" (US #5) in 1988, though overall sales gradually declined with each album selling less than the previous one. Prince continued to have success through the latter half of the 1980s, but his record sales declined and Warner Bros. executives became concerned about his output; his image was tarnished by the failure of later film ventures, his refusal to participate in "We Are The World," and the sacking of Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman. The 1985 album Around the World in a Day held No. 1 for three weeks and peaked at No. 5 in the UK, selling seven million copies despite minimal promotion; Parade (1986), the soundtrack for Prince's film Under the Cherry Moon, peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard chart and No. 2 on the R&B album charts, and the single "Kiss" reached No. 1 in the US and became a radio staple. Prince's next project began as a concept double-album called Dream Factory, then evolved into a solo album under the pseudonym Camille, which he later combined into the ambitious three-album set Crystal Ball; due to lower sales, Prince's manager Steve Fargnoli and Warner Bros. president Mo Ostin doubted its commercial viability, and after previewing it, Ostin insisted on reducing it to two records; Prince initially refused but eventually agreed and removed seven tracks, resulting in the 1987 release of Sign o' the Times, which peaked at No. 6 on the Billboard 200, sold 5 million copies, and had the title single "Sign o' the Times" reach No. 3 on the Hot 100; the follow-up "If I Was Your Girlfriend" flopped (reaching No. 12 on the R&B chart), but he scored hits with "U Got the Look" (#2 Hot 100, #11 R&B) and "I Could Never Take the Place of Your Man" (#10 Hot 100, #14 R&B). In 1985, Warner Bros. collaborated with View-Master to launch a children's video series, Kidsongs, produced by Together Again Productions and distributed by Warner Music Video for the educational market. From 1986 to 1987, Warner Bros. achieved greater success: Madonna's 1986 album True Blue produced three US number one hits and two top five singles, topped charts in over 28 countries (earning a Guinness Book of Records entry), and has sold over 25 million copies; Paul Simon burst back in late 1986 with Graceland, which initially faced commercial concerns due to its fusion of rock and African styles but became a resounding success, topping charts in many countries, reaching No. 3 in the US, producing two US Top 20 singles, becoming the best-selling American album of 1987, and selling over 5 million copies, winning the 1986 Grammy for 'Album of the Year' and the 1987 Grammy for 'Song of the Year' for the title track. In jazz, Warner Bros. signed Miles Davis after his break with Columbia; his 1986 comeback album Tutu was a major crossover hit, receiving rave reviews and winning a Grammy in 1987; Bob James also moved to the label in 1986 after nine years with Tappan Zee Records/Columbia, producing albums for Warner Bros. for the next sixteen years, with some of his back catalogue reissued in the mid-1990s. In the summer of 1986, Warner Bros. announced the reactivation of Reprise Records with its own promotions department, appointing former Warner Bros. Vice President of Promotion Richard Fitzgerald as label Vice President. In 1987, Prince recorded a pared-down funk album, The Black Album, which he withdrew in December just before release (despite 500,000 copies being printed); its replacement, Lovesexy (1988), reached No. 11 on the Billboard album chart and No. 1 in the UK. Prince rebounded in 1989 with the Batman film soundtrack, which sold over eleven million copies, reached No. 1 on the Billboard album chart, and produced four hit singles, including "Batdance," which topped both the Hot 100 and R&B charts. R.E.M., a 'cult' band that built a strong following in the US and internationally during the 1980s (partly due to innovative music videos), was signed to IRS Records for most of the decade and achieved mainstream success in 1987 with the album Document, their first to sell over one million copies; frustrated by IRS's poor international distribution, they signed with Warner Bros. when their contract expired in 1988; their Warner debut, Green, earned a platinum certification and sold over 4 million copies worldwide, with "Stand" becoming their first US hit single. In 1989, after guitarist Ricky Wilson's death, the B-52s returned to prominence with Cosmic Thing, a Top 5 hit in the US (#4) and UK (#2), reaching No. 1 in Australia, and scoring three consecutive hit singles: "Love Shack" (#3 US, #1 Australia), "Roam" (US #3), and "Deadbeat Club" (US #30). In early 1989, Madonna signed a Pepsi endorsement deal and debuted her single "Like a Prayer" in a commercial titled "Make a Wish," the first time a pop single debuted in an advertisement and the first such commercial to receive a worldwide satellite premiere; the music video premiered on MTV the following day and generated heated criticism due to its provocative religious imagery, leading to Pepsi withdrawing the ad and canceling the deal, though Madonna retained her $5 million advance; the controversy increased interest in the single and album, which became Madonna's seventh US number one hit and topped charts in over 30 countries, with the album selling fifteen million copies worldwide. In 1989, Time Inc. acquired Warner Communications and merged the two into Time Warner for a deal valued at $14 billion. After a period of stability in the competitive American music industry, the death of Steve Ross in late 1992 marked the beginning of major upheaval at Warner Bros. Records. R.E.M.'s second Warner album, Out of Time (1991), topped charts in both the US and the UK, produced two major hits—"Losing My Religion" reached #4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became a hit internationally, and "Shiny Happy People" was a Top 10 hit in both the US and the UK—and won three Grammy Awards. Prince's 1990s career was mixed; he scored more hits and renewed his contract in 1992, but tensions with Warner Bros. escalated, culminating in a public legal battle and his eventual departure. Although his film Graffiti Bridge was critically panned and a box office failure, the album of the same name reached No. 6 on both the Billboard Hot 200 and R&B album chart and produced two US Top 20 singles. Diamonds and Pearls (1991) became one of his biggest albums, selling 9 million records, reaching No. 3 in the US, No. 2 in the UK, and No. 1 in Australia, with five of the six singles becoming hits, including "Cream," which became his fifth US No. 1. Prince was appointed a vice-president of Warner Bros. Records in 1992 but soon regretted it; his next album, identified by the cryptic symbol on the cover later defined as "The Love Symbol," peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard 200 and sold 5 million copies worldwide, but tensions increased. Warner Bros. wanted to release "7" as the next single, but Prince pushed for "My Name Is Prince," which was a minor hit (#36 Hot 100, #23 R&B); "Sexy MF" was censored in the US due to an expletive in the chorus and did not enter the US Top 50, though it reached Top 5 in the UK and Australia; when released, "7" became the only major US hit from the album, peaking at No. 7. Following the 1993 3-disc compilation The Hits/The B-Sides, Prince stopped using his first name and began using only the "Love Symbol," drawing media ridicule; because the symbol has no verbal equivalent, he was often called "The Artist Formerly Known as Prince." By 1994, relations with the label had reached an impasse—WEA canceled its distribution deal with Paisley Park, effectively ending the label's operations. His single "The Most Beautiful Girl in the World" (1994) reached No. 3 in the US and topped charts throughout Europe, becoming his biggest hit single. Prince had prepared two new albums, Come and The Gold Experience; an early version of Come was rejected, but Warner Bros. eventually accepted both, though they refused to release them simultaneously. Prince launched a legal action to terminate his contract and gain ownership of his master recordings and publicly displayed the word "SLAVE" on his right cheek. Come (1994) was moderately successful in the US (#15, gold record), with the single "Let it go" reaching No. 10 on the R&B chart, though it was a major hit in the UK, debuting at No. 1. In November, a limited edition of The Black Album was released but was already widely bootlegged, sold poorly, and was soon deleted. The Gold Experience (1995) was praised by some reviewers as Prince's best effort since Sign o' the Times, including "The Most Beautiful Girl in the World" and producing two other charting singles, "I Hate U" (US #11) and "Gold" (UK #10). Prince's career with Warner Bros. ended with Chaos and Disorder (1996), compiled to end his contract; it was one of his least successful releases but reached No. 26 in the US and No. 14 in the UK and produced one minor hit, "Dinner With Delores" (#36 UK). Prince subsequently released recordings on his own NPG label (via EMI) before signing with Universal Music in 2005. R.E.M.'s Automatic for the People (1992) cemented their status as one of the top bands of the period, reached No. 1 in the UK and No. 2 in the US, sold over 10 million copies worldwide, and generated three US hit singles: "Drive," "Man on the Moon," and "Everybody Hurts." In 1992, Warner Bros. faced one of its most serious controversies over the provocative recording "Cop Killer."

Prince's career with Warner Bros. concluded with the release of *Chaos and Disorder* in 1996, a compilation made specifically to end his contract, which was one of his least successful albums but reached No. 26 in the US and No. 14 in the UK, producing one minor hit, "Dinner With Delores" (UK #36). After leaving Warner Bros., Prince released music on his own NPG label through EMI before signing with Universal Music in 2005. R.E.M.'s *Automatic for the People* (1992) became their most successful album, reaching No. 1 in the UK and No. 2 in the US, selling over 10 million copies worldwide, and generating three US hit singles: "Drive," "Man on the Moon," and "Everybody Hurts." In 1992, Warner Bros. faced a major controversy over the song "Cop Killer" by Body Count, a rap metal band led by Ice-T, which referenced the Rodney King case and was released just before the 1992 Los Angeles Riots. The song sparked national outrage, with conservative groups calling for a boycott of Time Warner products, President George H. W. Bush denouncing the label, executives receiving death threats, stockholders threatening to withdraw, and the New Zealand police commissioner attempting to ban it. Ice-T later reissued the album without "Cop Killer," and in January 1993, Warner Bros. made an undisclosed deal to release Ice-T from his contract and return the Body Count master tapes. As a result, Warner Bros. distanced itself from gangsta rap and in late 1995 sold its 50% stake in Interscope Records and Death Row Records (home to Tupac Shakur and Snoop Dogg) to Jimmy Iovine and Ted Field, who soon aligned Interscope with Universal Music Group, forming Interscope-Geffen-A&M, still run by Iovine. In 1994–1995, Warner Bros. experienced internal conflict centered on chairman Robert J. Morgado and his successor Michael J. Fuchs. Ostin, who had reported directly to Time Warner executives, resisted Morgado’s plan to have him report to him and to implement a "slash-and-burn" restructuring, leading to his refusal to renew his contract and departure on December 31, 1994, though he remained a senior consultant until August 1995. His exit caused industry-wide shock and triggered an exodus of executives, including Lenny Waronker, who declined the role of chairman and later co-founded DreamWorks Records with Ostin. Danny Goldberg, who had been president, left in August 1995 after settling a $20 million contract, and Russ Thyret was promoted to vice-chairman in January 1995 and later to chairman, CEO, and label president. Gerald Levin forced Morgado to resign in May 1995, replacing him with Fuchs, who dismissed Doug Morris a month later, sparking a $50 million breach of contract suit and the dissolution of Warner Music US. Morris moved to MCA Records. Despite these changes, many artists nurtured by Ostin and Waronker left the label as contracts expired; Ry Cooder was dropped in 1995 and Randy Newman joined DreamWorks, commenting that he had sent a resignation letter and hadn’t heard back, noting the indifference of both those leaving and those joining. Van Dyke Parks remained a notable survivor, releasing albums including *Tokyo Rose* (1989), *Orange Crate Art* (1995), and *Moonlighting: Live at the Ash Grove* (1998), and in 2004 reunited with Brian Wilson to complete *Smile*, released on Nonesuch, which won a Grammy, reached the Top 20 in the US and Top 10 in the UK, earning a gold record. In early 2001, Warner Music Group underwent a major restructuring, eliminating about 600 positions, and replacing Thyret and Quartararo, as well as Reprise president Howie Klein, with Tom Whalley as head of Warner Bros. Records. Whalley appointed Jeff Ayeroff as Creative Director and Creative Consultant, a former Senior Vice-President and Creative Director from 1983 to 1986. In 2002, Linkin Park won the Grammy for Best Hard Rock Performance for "Crawling," was nominated for Best New Artist and Best Rock Album for *Hybrid Theory*, the best-selling album of 2001 worldwide, and in 2004 was nominated for Best Rock Instrumental Performance for "Session." In 2006, they won Best Rap/Sung Collaboration for "Numb/Encore" released under Warner Bros./Roc-A-Fella/Machine Shop. In 2003, amid management disputes, declining share prices, and concerns over digital file sharing, Time Warner decided to sell its music operations. In March 2004, the music assets were acquired by a private equity group led by Thomas H. Lee Partners, Lexa Partners (led by Edgar Bronfman Jr., who contributed $150 million from his Vivendi stake), Bain Capital, and Providence Equity Partners, with an option for Time Warner to buy them back. The group reportedly recouped their investment by May 2006 through dividends, refinancing, and a share offer in May 2005. Following the sale, Warner implemented a major restructuring in the first half of 2004, cutting $27 million, laying off over 1,000 staff, dropping 80 artists (over half the roster), and folding Elektra into Atlantic while absorbing its sub-label Nonesuch into Warner Records; Elektra was later revived in 2009 and became an independently managed label in mid-2018. A short public dispute with Madonna occurred during this period, though the label distanced itself from the conflict, as Madonna remained signed. In 2005, Warner Music Australia acquired the assets of the Australian Festival Mushroom Group, which originated as Festival Records in 1952 and was acquired by Rupert Murdoch in 1961, becoming a leading Australian record company. Festival had distribution deals with local labels like Spin and Clarion, later acquiring their masters. It had signed a distribution deal with Mushroom Records in the 1970s, which achieved major success with Skyhooks' debut album *Living in the Seventies*, the highest-selling Australian album at the time. After Gudinski moved distribution to EMI, Festival acquired 49% of Mushroom in 1993 and bought the remaining shares in 1998. In 2005, News Ltd sold the group and its archive (containing over 20,000 master tapes) to Warner Music Australia for AU$10 million. Following the divestiture, Warner Music Group licensed the Warner Bros. trademarks, though the license could be revoked if WMG came under a major motion picture studio control. In 2010, after a corporate shakeup and a 16% drop in third-quarter revenue, Whalley left. Rob Cavallo, previously WMG’s chief creative officer, became chairman of Warner Bros. Records, with Todd Moscowitz and Livia Tortella named co-presidents, Moscowitz as CEO and Tortella as COO. Moscowitz resigned in December 2012, and Cameron Stang, chairman and CEO of Warner/Chappell and a WMG board member, was named chairman and CEO; Tortella left six months later, and Stang resigned in 2016 after a "tumultuous tenure." Dan McCarroll, named president in 2013, left in 2017. Despite having ten Top 10 albums, the label's performance was uneven, with a market share increase attributed to the post-2016 sales of Prince and Bowie albums. In October 2017, Aaron Bay-Schuck and Tom Corson were named co-chairmen of Warner Bros. Records, with Bay-Schuck as CEO and Corson as COO; Corson joined in January 2018 and Bay-Schuck began in the fall of that year. In March 2019, the Warner Bros. headquarters moved from Burbank to downtown Los Angeles. On May 28, the label announced it changed its name to Warner Records and unveiled a new logo—replacing the Warner Bros. shield with a wordmark and black circle (both partially cut off at the bottom), designed to resemble the Earth, a record, and the Sun, with "artful simplicity and impactful typography suited to the digital world." The change was required due to the expiration of the 15-year license to use the Warner Bros. name and shield, which had been granted after Time Warner sold Warner Music Group in 2004 (now Warner Bros. Discovery since 2022). The new logo received mixed reviews, with critics and former employees lamenting the replacement of the 61-year-old Warner Bros. emblem. The record label's ISRC code remained "WB1." In 2018 and 2019, Warner increased its focus on catalog, releasing boxed sets for Green Day's *Nimrod* and Linkin Park's *Hybrid Theory*, and working with the estates of Mac Miller and the Ramones. In 2019, NLE Choppa launched a label with Warner; his 2020 album *Top Shotta* went platinum in the US and Canada. New records by Omar Apollo, Gorillaz, and Red Hot Chili Peppers were successful, and Dua Lipa's *Future Nostalgia* was a massive hit, becoming the 69th best-selling record in the US and the tenth best-seller worldwide in 2020, and the ninth best-seller in the US and sixth worldwide in 2021. The success of *Future Nostalgia* "bought more time" for Bay-Schuck and Corson to retool the artist roster. In 2021, Warner signed Zach Bryan and Benson Boone. In 2022, a partnership with SM Entertainment for K-pop girl group Aespa's global promotions was announced. Teddy Swims, signed in 2019, had a six-times platinum single in 2023 for "Lose Control." With Emily Armstrong, Linkin Park had its biggest hit in 15 years, and the IFPI named Boone's "viral as fuck" "Beautiful Things" the year's biggest single worldwide. In October 2023, Bryan's *American Heartbreak*, his Warner debut, hit platinum sales, and nine singles from the album were certified gold or platinum. In February of the following year, two more albums were released.

Facing pressure to expand its market share, the success of Future Nostalgia provided Bay-Schuck and Corson with additional time to reevaluate and retool the artist roster. In 2021, Warner signed Zach Bryan and Benson Boone, among other artists. A partnership with SM Entertainment for the global promotions of the K-pop girl group Aespa was announced in 2022. Teddy Swims, signed in 2019, achieved a six-times platinum single in 2023 with "Lose Control." With new singer Emily Armstrong, Linkin Park had its biggest hit in 15 years, and the international music industry trade group IFPI named Benson Boone's "viral as fuck" "Beautiful Things" as the year's biggest single worldwide. In October 2023, Bryan's debut album American Heartbreak, released on Warner, reached platinum sales, with nine singles from the album certified gold or platinum. In February of the following year, two additional albums and 16 singles achieved gold or platinum status. In an interview with Billboard, Bay-Schuck stated that Bryan represented the label's legacy: "No one was telling Prince what to do, no one was telling Madonna what to do. You give them advice, you challenge them, you insert your opinions where you can. But ultimately, those artists thrived because the label understood how to let them grow and mature and take swings on their own." In 2024, Warner Records ranked third in market share, marking the label's highest market share since 2018.
